paper_title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.

INTRODUCTION Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small changes in policy can alter future observations and amplify into closed-loop task failure. In embodied control, an action error changes the next physical state, modifies the next observation, and may place the policy outside the training distribution. Subsequent errors can therefore compound over the remainder of the trajectory [1], [2]. Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine visual perception, language grounding, and low-level control within single pretrained policy. OpenVLA provides an open 7B VLA with tokenized actions and pretrained vision-language backbone [3]. OpenVLA-OFT later demonstrated that continuous actions, action chunking, and optimized decoding can substantially improve success and inference efficiency [4]. These advances strengthen task acquisition, but do not remove the continual-learning problem: sequential fine-tuning can overwrite behavior required by earlier manipulation skills. Existing continual-learning strategies offer complementary trade-offs. Replay remains strong baseline but requires storing or regenerating previous observations. Expansion and routing methods isolate tasks but add modules or routing mechanisms. Parameter-regularization methods preserve previous solution but can restrict acquisition. Direct updatesuppression methods reduce future plasticity according to past update history, but can become too restrictive for large heterogeneous models. This work develops replay-free mechanism based on physical observation: parameters supporting correct behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory regions should become less plastic in later tasks. Unlike reference-based consolidation methods, the proposed Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP) does not penalize parameter displacement from previously stored checkpoint. Instead, similar to CLASSP [5], it uses accumulated historical importance to directly regulate future plasticity. Protection is therefore active from the first update of each subsequent learning stage and does not require storing reference copies of the adaptable parameters. This work contributes local policy-independent dynamicsrisk estimator derived from expert state-action trajectories. The resulting risk scores weight the historical importance of adaptable tensors, which is then used to regulate their future plasticity through tensor-specific AdamW learning rates. This mechanism suppresses the actual optimizer step rather than merely scaling raw gradients. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on continual learning for visionlanguage-action models and on importance-based plasticity control. Section III describes the sequential LIBERO evaluation protocol. Section IV motivates the dynamics-risk signal from the compounding-error perspective of imitation learning, and Section formalizes the replay-free continual learning problem. Section VI presents the DRAP method, including the KappaTune-based subnetwork selection, the local dynamicsrisk estimator, the risk-weighted tensor importance, and the tensor-specific learning-rate control. Section VII reports the experimental results, including ablations of KappaTune selection and of dynamics-risk weighting. Finally, Section VIII concludes and outlines directions for future work. II. RELATED WORK Recent continual-learning methods for vision-languageaction models primarily rely on architectural modularity, routing, replay, or parameter regularization. CLARE [6] autonomously expands and routes lightweight adapters, allowing new manipulation tasks to be learned without requiring task identifiers at deployment. Stellar VLA [7] instead models task and skill relationships in learned knowledge space and uses knowledge-guided expert routing, with limited replay, to reduce interference between sequentially learned behaviors. These approaches obtain stability by separating or routing task-specific capacity, whereas DRAP retains fixed model architecture and controls the plasticity of an existing trainable subnetwork. Among replay-free regularization methods, EWC [8], Synaptic Intelligence [9], Memory Aware Synapses [10], and RWalk [11] estimate the historical importance of model parameters and restrict subsequent changes to important parameters. EWC and RWalk employ reference-based quadratic penalties, while Synaptic Intelligence accumulates optimizationpath contributions and Memory Aware Synapses measures the sensitivity of the learned output function. Despite their different motivations, these importance estimators have been shown to be closely related to Fisher-information-based quantities [12]. DRAP differs by weighting sample-level actiongradient responsibility according to the estimated physical consequence of errors along the demonstrated trajectory. DRAP is most closely related to continual-learning methods that regulate future parameter plasticity according to historical importance. CLASSP [5] suppresses future updates using accumulated gradient magnitudes and optionally applies gradient threshold to promote sparse adaptation. Bayesian approaches such as uncertainty-guided continual learning [13], [14] similarly use parameter uncertainty to determine which model components should remain stable and which should retain greater plasticity. DRAP follows this general principle of importance-dependent plasticity, but replaces generic update history or posterior uncertainty with dynamics-risk-weighted, sample-level behavioral responsibility. The accumulated importance is defined at tensor level and directly scales tensorspecific AdamW learning rates. Thus, DRAP is inspired by CLASSPs adjustment-suppression principle, but uses different importance signal and optimizer interface. Reference-based methods adopt different protection mechanism. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) [8] estimates parameter importance using diagonal Fisher approximation and penalizes displacement from previous optimum. In contrast, DRAP does not store reference parameters or apply displacement penalty. Historical importance regulates plasticity immediately from the first update of each subsequent learning stage. Liu et al. [15] investigate continual learning with large pretrained VLAs by sequentially training across the ten tasks of each LIBERO suite. Their main finding is that pretrained models such as π0 and GR00T N1.5 can achieve little forgetting when combined with experience replay, and retain comparatively low forgetting even when the replay buffer contains only small fraction of the previous-task data. However, their zero-replay Sequential and EWC baselines on LIBERO-Object and LIBERO-10 still exhibit substantial negative backward transfer, indicating that pretraining alone does not prevent forgetting when earlier demonstrations are unavailable. Their protocol differs from ours in three respects. First, they train separate continual model for each LIBERO suite and learn the ten tasks within that suite sequentially, whereas our protocol updates one checkpoint across complete suites in the order Spatial, Object, and Goal. Second, their strongest retention results store transitions from previous tasks, while DRAP is evaluated without storing any previous-suite demonstrations. Third, they use different VLA architectures with LoRA-based or partially frozen fine-tuning, whereas we adapt KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA. The two settings therefore address complementary questions: their results show that pretrained VLAs exploit small replay buffers particularly well, whereas DRAP targets retention under strictly replay-free sequence of suite-level shifts. Since the replay-free setting is already difficult in both protocols, and our sequence additionally requires retention across suites that differ in layout, object identity, and goal semantics, we consider it demanding test of forgetting. KappaTune [16] uses the matrix condition number as scale-invariant proxy for information encoding in neural tensors. Its central hypothesis is that tensors with larger condition numbers contain more strongly differentiated singular directions and are therefore more likely to encode specialized pretrained information. KappaTune preserves these tensors and concentrates adaptation on tensors with smaller condition numbers, which are treated as safer sources of plasticity. III. EVALUATION PROTOCOL LIBERO provides benchmark for knowledge transfer and lifelong robot learning across Spatial, Object, Goal, and LongHorizon suites [17]. LIBERO results depend strongly on the training protocol. OpenVLA-OFT reports 97.1% average success rate using four independently fine-tuned policies, one for each of the Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long-Horizon suites [4]. It also reports 96.8% for single policy jointly trained on data from all four suites. These settings evaluate suitespecific or joint multi-suite acquisition. This work instead evaluates sequential continual learning without replay. single checkpoint is trained successively on Spatial, Object and Goal, with only the current suite available at each stage. After every stage, the checkpoint is evaluated on all suites observed so far. The resulting lower-triangular success matrix therefore measures both new-suite acquisition and backward retention under closed-loop control. As shown by the standard sequential-training baseline, this protocol presents challenging catastrophic-forgetting setting, with performance on earlier suites degrading substantially after adaptation to subsequent suites. IV. COMPOUNDING ERRORS AND DYNAMICS-RISK MOTIVATION Behavior cloning is affected by covariate shift because policy-generated actions modify future states and observations (4) (5) (6) (7) In physical AI, [1], [2]. small action error can move the robot away from the demonstrated trajectory, expose the policy to unfamiliar observations, and increase the probability of subsequent errors. these deviations can compound over closed-loop rollout and cause task failure even when the per step prediction error remains small. DRAP addresses this problem by assigning greater importance to demonstration samples at which the local physical dynamics are more likely to amplify state perturbation. The risk estimator is inspired by Lyapunovs indirect method, which studies nonlinear systems locally through linearization [18], and by contraction analysis, which examines the local convergence or divergence of neighboring trajectories [19]. DRAP uses this local differential perspective to rank demonstration samples according to their estimated one-step perturbation amplification. The resulting dynamics-risk score is relative sensitivity indicator, its purpose is to identify trajectory regions where preserving accurate policy behavior may be particularly important because small deviations can have larger downstream physical consequences. CONCLUSION This work takes first step toward physics-informed plasticity control by introducing DRAP, replay-free method for continual learning in physical AI. DRAP estimates tensor importance from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk and uses the accumulated importance to regulate tensor-specific AdamW learning rates during subsequent adaptation. Intuitively, DRAP suppresses future updates to tensors that were important for predicting expert actions at samples where errors are more strongly amplified by the physical dynamics. Sequential LIBERO experiments showed that standard finetuning suffers severe catastrophic forgetting, while the physically ungrounded method, EWC, provides only partial retention. DRAP achieved the strongest stability-plasticity balance when combined with KappaTune. KappaTune restricts adaptation to structurally selected subnetwork, while DRAP distributes plasticity within that subnetwork according to historical, dynamics-risk-weighted responsibility. The ablation without KappaTune confirmed that broader plasticity improves initial acquisition but increases later interference. Sequential LIBERO experiments showed that standard finetuning suffers severe catastrophic forgetting, while EWC provides only partial retention. KappaTune+DRAP achieved the strongest stability-plasticity balance. KappaTune restricts adaptation to selected subnetwork, while DRAP regulates plasticity within that subnetwork according to accumulated historical importance. The ablation without KappaTune showed that broader adaptable parameter space supports strong initial acquisition but substantially increases later interference. The uniform-risk ablation showed that importancedependent plasticity accounts for most of DRAPs benefit, imwhile dynamics-risk weighting provides an additional provement in retention without impairing new-suite acquisition. These results support the hypothesis that continual learning in physical AI should consider both model sensitivity and the physical consequences of behavioral errors. Future work will improve the dynamics-risk estimator by incorporating the control pathway, online estimation, multi-step perturbation propagation, and contact-aware dynamics. It will also investigate the CLASSP-inspired update threshold and evaluate DRAP over longer continual-learning sequences.
